Looking at it from another direction:

- You play Charming Lobby as a vampire.

Good point.

Probably a better ruling would draw the line between
"things that happen because the card is played" and "things
that happen because the card is in play". So if an ally can
play a card "as a vampire", then the effects of the card
go off as if he were a vampire. For other effects, including
effects generated by that card remaining in play, he is not
treated as a vampire.

Moving the line thus would put Talaq in danger from his
Burst of Sunlight strike.

It would also allow the Herald to play Charming Lobby in
order to call a referendum.

Neither of those are true currently.

I'll put this on the RT list for review.



Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 10 Feb 2002 01:14:34 GMT, Johan Lundstrom wrote:

>What is the reason some rules are so written in stone that they can't
>even in principle be broken by card text, and how do we differentaite
>them from those rules which can be overridden by card text?

They are differentiated by being called "Golden Rules". The second of
these gives cards permission to override any of the other rules.

There are higher-order metarules (rules about rules) such as
tournament rules but these are not relevant in this case.

Andrew

Messages.Author: The Fanboy
Messages.Body:
> So a (hypothetical) ally with the text "This ally can call
> referendums" wouldn't in fact be able to call referendums?

No. In this case, the card text explicitly allows the ally to call
referendums.

Herald does not explicitly allow it - yes, his ability allows him to
play the Charming Lobby, but it doesn't allow him to call referendums.

Let's say there's an ally - Akashic Mage. Let's say he has a
restriction - cannot bleed. Then let's give him the special - may
play cards requiring basic Dominate as if he were a vampire of
capacity 4.

Could he Govern? No. Because he can't bleed.

Consider all allies to have explicit card text saying "May not call
referendums" and you're all set.

Fanboy

Messages.Author: Nystulc

Francois Gombault:

>And for the sake of completeness, and since you're in the process of

>
>Could this ally block a Slaughtering the Herd action (allies can't block) ?
>Could this ally block an action modified by Daring the Dawn (vampires
>can't block) ?

In both cases, he must be treated as an ally in terms of deciding if he can
attempt to block. He declares the block attempt first, and does so as an ally.
Then, to determine if the block is successful, he adds intercept as a vampire.

It would be a bit more tricky, I guess, if he were to play some Auspex card
that granted him block ability. For instance, supposing could play Superior
Auspex cards, what if he played Eagle's Sight? Similarly could he play some
hypothetical Auspex version of WWEF (assume it is identical to WWEF but has no
Do-Not-Replace restriction).

-- John Whelan

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
vte...@white-wolf.com writes:

>Joshua Duffin wrote:
>> I think this imaginary Auspex-playing ally *would* be
>> able to block a 1-stealth Daring the Dawn action with
>> Enhanced Senses, though, because although he plays the
>> Enhanced Senses as a vampire, he is no longer a vampire
>> once the Enhanced Senses is done being played, and so
>> will be (again) eligible to block and now have enough
>> intercept to block as well.

>Can't play Eagle's Sight as a vampire - since vampires cannot
>block and therefore would not need intercept (and you can
>only play Eagle's Sight if you're blocking and need intercept).

Something is awry with the game mechanics of these "as a
vampire" cards. This is supposed to model minions who can
create effects similar to those of vampires with disciplines
even though they're not vampires and don't actually have the
disciplines. In no present case is the minion "slumming" as
a vampire - they should *never* get the peculiar advantages
and disadvantages of vampires during the process of playing
a card. There should be no "when do they go back to being
an ally" decision because they should never stop in the first
place. If some Tremeresque magus had an ability to actually
become a vampire for the duration of an action, it should need
explicit text a la Grandest Trick.

Surely with the extensive play and rules experience of LSJ,
the Rules Team, and WW, somebody can figure out how to
do this right? Correspondance mages or vicissitude-enhanced
ghouls should not lose their Auspex-mimicking abilities
because it's daytime; that's incredibly counterintuitive.

In regards to the original Charming Lobby question, I
now think the herald should be barred - because Charming
Lobby doesn't grant the ability to call a vote you can't
call in the first place, right? E.g. Igo can't CL to call
a Parity Shift. CL might need errata to make this clear.

P.S. What happened to the interpretation that CL calls
a vote with no effect other than to autopass the next
vote? That would solve the problem - the Herald could
CL, but somebody else must call the actual vote. I see
no problem with skilled lobbyists who can't actually
call votes - that's what most of them are.
